title: RAKER'S MORNING
logSummary: A wrong tide in the third pan, a pegged line to the black beach, and a Plumb painting Saltrow's own dyke.

stages.note: Rake the third pan with Matron Ansel
Rake salt from the third pan  {n} / {of}
Raise the Alidade and read the Gauge
stages.log: Read the Gauge: Sluice 3, open at 0.4 m.

stages.note: Tell Ansel what the Gauge reads
stages.log: Told Ansel. The pan is not on its map.

stages.note: Make a bundle of Reed arrows
Ask Mise on the breakwater what came ashore
stages.log: Mise counted nine Pegs in at the fourth bell.

stages.note: Cross the Peg line without being Flagged
stages.logSeen: Crossed the transect. Seen by a Peg.

stages.note: Climb trig pillar T1 on the Organ Shelf
Sight T2 and T6 from the pillar  {n} / {of}
stages.log: Sighted T2 and T6. The first triangle is on the sheet.

stages.note: Come down on the Plumb through the lee ditch
stages.log: Reached the pan-edge station through the rush.

stages.note: Topple the Plumb: two hits on the level vial
Pry the bob while it is down
stages.log: Pried the bob off its cable.
Ansel gave the Guild Whites and thirty salt.

closing.note: The Brazier at T1 can be kindled
closing.logEnd: The Plumb is down. The line is still on Saltrow's dyke.

lines: You're late. The crust on the third pan
set an hour ago. Take the other rake.
The sun's one hand above the breakwater.
That's on time. You were early.
I'm sixty-four. Early is all I have left.
Ten baskets before the porters come.
Ten baskets. Wind's at 045 and steady.
It'll dry as fast as we lift it.

scenes.where: the third pan, after the tenth basket

lines: That's ten. Your share is in the tally.
Salt in the hand is the only kind
that counts.
Ten in the tally and twenty on my belt.
Thirty buys cord and leaves change.

scenes.where: the third pan, as the water comes in

lines: Brea. The water.
That's Sluice 3. It isn't due
until the noon bell.
It's open a full hand,
and the tide is nowhere near.
Keep your rake. I'll read it.

scenes.where: the third pan, after the Sighting

lines: The Gauge has the tide at 0.4 metres.
It opened Sluice 3 on that.
It has never opened at 0.4.
Forty years I have stood in this pan.
It isn't broken. The sea is where
it says. The ground has moved,
and the pan was never in its book.
A morning's salt, gone back to brine.
Can you bargain with it?
That is your office.
I can bargain with its clock.
Not with its map.
It's the newest. My mother's house
cut it. Sixty years of salt off it.
Sixty years is yesterday to them.
By the Datum that pan is
752 years late.
Late by a bell, once or twice.
Never open on a low tide.
One bell late is a clock.
This is a level. Different fault,
and the worse one.
Give me one day. I want to see
what else it is reading.
Then go armed. Mise has been ringing
since first light. Something walked
up the beach in the dark.

scenes.where: the third pan, as Brea turns to go

lines: And you have twelve arrows.
That is a short day. There's cane
standing at the dyke. Cut it.
Six stalks, six shafts.
I'll cut on the way.
Reckoner. I counted them in
at the fourth bell. Nine Pegs,
out of the surf, in file.
Nine. Where did they start hammering?
At the pans. They've pegged a line
clean down to the black beach,
straight as a taut cord.
Pans to the beach is bearing 132.
Pegs don't walk a line for themselves.
Where's the Plumb?
I haven't seen one. My eyes are
sixty-eight years old, and the lamp
was in them all night.
Then I'll look from higher. The pillar
on the Organ Shelf sees both ends
of that line.
Mind the peg-heads. Cross a lit line
near a Plumb and it turns
its lamp on you.
Inside twenty paces of it, yes.
I'll cross wide.
The meadow won't hide you.
The reed at the Glass rim will,
while the wind is in it.
The wind's good for an hour yet.
Ring twice if they turn.
I watched it go over from this step.
And I can see the paint from here.
Vermilion, a quarter of a metre tall,
the whole length of the outer dyke.
Saltrow is marked for cutting down.
Marked by what?
You put the thing on its back.
A Plumb only holds the brush.
The line stays until that ground
is made true.
Then this house needs more than
a Reckoner who moves pans.
Take the Guild Whites. Scout's cut.
And thirty salt. You are on
the house's business now.
Thirty salt and a hat.
I have been paid worse.
Rest first. Your cistern is full
and the pitch is dry. The pans
will be here when you wake.
They will. Where they are,
not where it wants them.

scenes.where: the breakwater lamp, after the Plumb is down

lines: The lamp's lit. First night in
forty years I have wanted
it brighter.
It carries eighty paces.
That is what you need it for.
Anything inside that, ring.
And outside it?
Outside it is my office.

breaAlone.about: Brea's own turns in the field: one card each, shown as a subtitle when its trigger first happens. Each trigger shows once.

lines: Ash. I slept past the Brazier.
The house kite's up already.
Line's streaming to 225.
Good drying wind.
One Gauge, at Sluice 3, lamp calm.
It thinks this is routine.
Six stalks. Straight enough.
Peg-heads every three paces, all lit.
That is a live line.
Meadow. Pretty, and no use at all.
It doesn't hide anybody.
Rush to the shoulder, two hands of wind.
This will do.
One lamp out. It can hammer blind.
Across. Nobody the wiser.
Flagged. Eight seconds of everything
inside sixty paces knowing
where I stand.
T1. Fourteen metres of basalt stair
and one white post.
Somebody liked a view.
T2, on Ninewalls Rise.
Bearing {bearing}.
T6, on the West Rim.
Bearing {bearing}.
Two bearings and a baseline.
That is a triangle,
and the sheet fills in.
The Ring, the Scar, the rim.
Three things on this island
that are dead straight or dead round.
There. Pan-edge station, bearing {bearing}.
One Plumb, and the morning's Pegs
standing round it.
It's painting our outer dyke.
That line sits two hands
under the dyke top.
Everything above the paint
is what it means to take off.
The lee ditch brings me in
under its lamp. Two on the vial,
then the bob while it's down.
One. It's hunting for level.
It has chimed. Here come the Pegs.
Down. Four seconds. The bob, now.
That's the bob. It swings at
nobody now.
One Plumb off its legs.
The line is still on the wall.
